set1.q: Which test in the lung cancer workup is noted to be not sensitive?
opts: Bronchoscopic biopsy is one of the standard ways to obtain tissue, chosen by the location of the nodule, and tissue is what confirms the diagnosis. Tell: the weak link of the workup is sputum cytology.

Correct. Sputum cytology is listed among the additional tests but is not sensitive, so it is not relied on to find lung cancer. The exception is squamous cell carcinoma in the central bronchi, which, unlike the other types, can be caught with sputum testing.

Contrast computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen is the standard first study of the workup, followed by biopsy or interventional treatment. Tell: the test flagged as not sensitive is sputum cytology.

Positron emission tomography is part of the standard workup and staging, showing highly metabolic tissue and lymph involvement, although inflammation can also take up the tracer. Tell: its pitfall is false brightness; the test flagged as not sensitive is sputum cytology.

set1.q: Which person without symptoms meets every lung cancer screening criterion?
opts: Correct. Screening is for adults without symptoms aged 55 to 80 with at least a 30 pack-year history who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years. A current smoker in their early sixties with 40 pack-years meets every part and is screened every year with low-dose chest computed tomography.
Quitting more than 15 years ago takes a former smoker out of screening, however heavy the pack-year history. Tell: a former smoker qualifies only when the quit date falls within the last 15 years.
ruled out by a stated finding
At 45 this person is below the screening age band despite the heavy smoking history. Tell: age, pack-years and smoking status must all fit, and a person in their forties is too young.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: Which laboratory test in the lung cancer workup would reveal hypercalcemia?
opts: Pulmonary function tests are an additional consideration that assesses the lungs themselves; they are not a blood test and give no calcium level. Tell: hypercalcemia is a laboratory finding on the comprehensive metabolic panel.

Correct. The lab workup lists a complete blood count with differential, a comprehensive metabolic panel including calcium, and an alkaline phosphatase. The calcium on the metabolic panel is how hypercalcemia shows up, a paraneoplastic finding linked particularly to squamous cell carcinoma.
A complete blood count with differential is part of the lab workup, but it counts blood cells and does not report calcium. Tell: calcium is measured on the comprehensive metabolic panel.

Alkaline phosphatase is listed as its own laboratory test in the workup, separate from the calcium measured on the comprehensive metabolic panel. Tell: hypercalcemia is read from the metabolic panel's calcium value.

set1.q: When a new solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm is evaluated, which result carries a recommendation for referral to a subspecialist such as a pulmonologist or thoracic surgeon?
opts: Negative or mild uptake returns the nodule to the same surveillance scans as the very low probability group, without the referral flag. Tell: referral goes with moderate or intense uptake, the branch that leads to tissue.

This evaluation covers new solid nodules of 8 to 30 mm, and a nodule under 6 mm is generally not concerning unless the patient is high risk. Tell: small size argues against referral; the flag sits on strong uptake or high probability.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Referral to a subspecialist such as a pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, interventional radiologist or oncologist is recommended for moderate or intense uptake on positron emission tomography, and for a high clinical probability of malignancy. Those nodules go on to biopsy or resection.

A very low probability nodule is followed with surveillance scans at 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 24 months, and no subspecialist referral is flagged on that path. Tell: referral attaches to the high-probability and high-uptake branches.

set1.q: In lung disease, carcinoid syndrome comes mainly from which tumor?
opts: Correct. For lung causes, carcinoid syndrome comes mainly from a bronchial carcinoid, one of the rarer lung tumor types. Release of serotonin from the tumor cells causes flushing, apparent cyanosis, wheezing, diarrhea, cramps, hepatomegaly and thickening of the pulmonic and tricuspid valves.
The classic endocrine syndrome of small cell carcinoma is excess antidiuretic hormone with hyponatremia, not serotonin excess. Tell: carcinoid syndrome from the lung comes from a bronchial carcinoid.
Squamous cell carcinoma is linked particularly to hypercalcemia among the paraneoplastic syndromes. Tell: flushing and serotonin excess point to a bronchial carcinoid.
The paraneoplastic issues of adenocarcinoma come as later systemic signs, and it is not the lung source of carcinoid syndrome. Tell: carcinoid syndrome from the lung means a bronchial carcinoid.

set1.q: Why is large cell carcinoma a diagnosis of exclusion among non-small cell lung cancers?
opts: Mucin on a mucicarmine stain points to adenocarcinoma, and negative staining may point to large cell carcinoma. Tell: large cell is defined by what it lacks, including mucin.
Sputum testing catches squamous cell carcinoma, the central bronchial type, unlike the other lung cancers. Tell: large cell carcinoma is peripheral and needs biopsy with histology to confirm it.

Crushed cells on biopsy describe small cell carcinoma, a fragile tumor with small cells, no nucleoli and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio. Tell: large cell has cells about three times larger than baseline and no specific marker.

Correct. Large cell carcinoma lacks specific genetic or histology markers, so it is diagnosed by exclusion among the non-small cell types. It is anaplastic, undifferentiated and pleomorphic, which separates it from adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, and histology must confirm the anaplastic tissue.

set1.q: What does large cell carcinoma typically show on chest computed tomography?
opts: Correct. Large cell carcinoma shows a large, cavitated mass on chest computed tomography, typically in the periphery rather than centrally like squamous cell carcinoma, often with angiogenesis, its own blood supply. Biopsy with histology is still needed to confirm the anaplastic tissue.
A central mass obstructing a bronchus fits squamous cell carcinoma, which causes cough, wheezing, hemoptysis and atelectasis. Tell: large cell carcinoma is the peripheral type.
Popcorn-looking calcification marks a hamartoma, a benign nodule. Tell: large cell carcinoma is a large peripheral mass that cavitates, not a calcified nodule.
A smoothly marginated nodule with internal fat is consistent with a hamartoma, a benign finding. Tell: large cell carcinoma shows a large cavitated peripheral mass.

set1.q: Which central lung cancer is usually metastatic by the time it is diagnosed?
opts: Adenocarcinoma is peripheral, found in the mid-lung and periphery, so it does not fit a central tumor. Tell: the central type that is usually metastatic at diagnosis is small cell.
ruled out by a stated finding

Large cell carcinoma forms in the periphery and metastasizes to unusual sites such as the small intestine and bowel. Tell: a central location rules it out; small cell is central and usually metastatic at diagnosis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Small cell carcinoma is central, infiltrates the mucosa and develops insidiously, so over 70% of patients are already metastatic to the liver, bone or brain before detection. That is why it is usually metastatic by the time of diagnosis.

Squamous cell carcinoma is central too, but it is the type that can be caught with sputum testing, and it spreads by local invasion and lymphangitic spread to hilar nodes. Tell: central and metastatic at diagnosis points to small cell.

set1.q: Which signs appear later in adenocarcinoma, after the respiratory symptoms?
opts: Cough and shortness of breath are early presenting symptoms, often persistent and without signs of infection. Tell: respiratory symptoms come first, while bone pain and weight loss come later.
Hemoptysis and chest tightness or pain are on the list of first, respiratory symptoms. Tell: the later signs are systemic, such as bone pain and weight loss.
Fatigue and chest tightness belong to the early symptom list of adenocarcinoma. Tell: later disease shows bone pain, weight loss and paraneoplastic issues.

Correct. Adenocarcinoma is mostly asymptomatic early, then usually presents with respiratory symptoms first: cough, shortness of breath, chest tightness or pain, hemoptysis and fatigue. Bone pain, weight loss and other systemic, paraneoplastic issues are the later signs.

set1.q: What is the five-year survival for lung cancer in the United States?
opts: About 5% understates the United States figure, where 17 to 18% of patients are alive five years after diagnosis; the outlook is described as worse only in the rest of the world. Tell: the United States number sits in the high teens, still one of the lowest of all cancers.

Correct. Lung cancer has one of the lowest five-year survival prognoses: about 17 to 18% of patients in the United States are alive five years after diagnosis, and the outlook is even worse in the rest of the world. Much of the reason is that symptoms appear only once the disease is advanced or already metastatic.

Thirty percent is closer to the share of male cancer deaths that lung cancer causes, more than 30%, than to its five-year survival of 17 to 18%. Tell: the death share in men is over 30%; the survival figure is under 20%.

A 60% five-year survival would make lung cancer one of the more survivable cancers, the reverse of its standing: 17 to 18% of patients in the United States reach five years. Tell: late presentation keeps lung cancer near the bottom of the survival table.

set1.q: Which finding sends a patient to a diagnostic workup for lung cancer instead of routine screening?
opts: A heavy pack-year history is a risk factor that makes an adult without symptoms a candidate for annual low-dose screening; it is not a symptom. Tell: risk factors route a patient to screening, while symptoms route a patient to a diagnostic workup.

Smoking now is part of the screening criteria for a high-risk adult without symptoms, so it points toward screening rather than away from it. Tell: a symptom such as hemoptysis is what moves a patient out of the screening pathway.

Radon exposure is a listed risk factor for lung cancer, but it is not a symptom and does not trigger a diagnostic workup by itself. Tell: look for a symptom such as hemoptysis, persistent cough or weight loss.

Correct. Screening is meant for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule. Hemoptysis is one of the presenting symptoms, along with persistent cough, dysphagia, wheezing or shortness of breath and systemic symptoms, that call for a workup for possible lung cancer instead.

set1.q: Popcorn calcification in a lung nodule points to which lesion?
opts: A healed granuloma, an inflammatory lesion, is the smoothly marginated nodule with central calcification, not popcorn calcification. Tell: a central dot of calcium suggests a granuloma; popcorn clusters suggest a hamartoma.

Adenocarcinoma appears as a suspicious solid spiculated nodule in the periphery, and the calcification patterns grouped as malignant are ground-glass and eccentric. Tell: popcorn calcification sits on the benign side of the chart.

A carcinoid tumor is one of the rare lung tumor types, and a bronchial carcinoid is the lung source of carcinoid syndrome; popcorn calcification is not its described sign. Tell: popcorn calcification is the hamartoma pattern.

Correct. Benign nodules tend to have well-defined borders and may contain fatty tissue or calcifications; popcorn-looking calcification means a hamartoma, a connective tissue growth. On computed tomography a hamartoma is a smoothly marginated solid nodule with internal fat and calcification.

set1.q: A 4.5 cm lung cancer has not spread to any lymph nodes or distant sites; which stage is it?
opts: Stage 1B stops at 4 cm: it is a node-negative tumor more than 3 cm but no more than 4 cm in its greatest dimension. Tell: 4.5 cm crosses the 4 cm line into stage 2A.

Correct. Stage 2A is a tumor more than 4 cm but no more than 5 cm in its greatest dimension that has not spread to any lymph nodes. A 4.5 cm node-negative tumor without metastasis fits exactly, T2b N0 M0.
Stage 2B starts above 5 cm for a node-negative tumor, or adds peribronchial or hilar nodes to a tumor up to 5 cm. Tell: 4.5 cm with no nodes stays in stage 2A.

Stage 3A needs a tumor over 7 cm, invasion of structures such as the diaphragm or mediastinum, or nodal spread with a large tumor or to the mediastinal nodes. Tell: none of that is present, so the stage is 2A.

set1.q: Biopsy confirms lung cancer in a patient who is fit for surgery but unfit for lobectomy; which treatment is used?
opts: Radiofrequency ablation sits on the path for patients unfit for any surgery, with stereotactic ablative or conventional radical radiotherapy. Tell: this patient is fit for surgery, just not a full lobectomy, so a segmentectomy is used.

Correct. In a patient fit for surgery, image-guided biopsy that confirms malignancy leads to lobectomy, or to anatomical segmentectomy when the patient is unfit for lobectomy. A segment resection removes a larger portion of a lobe than a wedge resection but less than the entire lobe.

Pneumonectomy removes the entire lung, more than a lobectomy, so it is no answer for a patient who cannot tolerate losing a whole lobe. Tell: unfit for lobectomy calls for a smaller resection, the anatomical segmentectomy.

Completion lobectomy follows a wedge resection with an on-table frozen section in a patient who can have a lobectomy. Tell: removing the whole lobe is exactly what this patient cannot tolerate; a segmentectomy spares part of it.

set1.q: Why does high uptake on positron emission tomography not prove that a nodule is malignant?
opts: The reverse is true: highly metabolic tumor cells take up the sugar tracer avidly, which is why uptake suggests malignancy. Tell: the false alarm comes from inflammation taking up the tracer too.

Uptake reflects how much sugar tracer metabolically active cells take up, not the size of the nodule, which computed tomography measures. Tell: a bright nodule may be cancer or inflammation, whatever its size.

Correct. Positron emission tomography uses a radioactive sugar, fludeoxyglucose, that highly metabolic cells take up, suggesting malignancy. Inflammatory conditions can also show high uptake, so uptake does not rule them out and tissue is still needed. Low or normal uptake is a good sign.
The tracer is not a sugar
The tracer is a radioactive sugar, fludeoxyglucose, taken up by highly metabolic cells. Tell: the limit is not the tracer itself but that inflamed tissue is also metabolically active and takes it up.

set1.q: Which cells lining the bronchioles give rise to the hormone-secreting paraneoplastic symptoms of small cell carcinoma?
opts: Type I pneumocytes are thin cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange; they line the alveoli, not the bronchioles, and do not secrete hormones. Tell: hormone-type symptoms trace back to neuroendocrine cells.

Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant inside the alveoli and are the usual origin of adenocarcinoma, not of the hormone-driven syndromes of small cell carcinoma. Tell: surfactant cells give adenocarcinoma; hormone-secreting cells give small cell symptoms.

The capillary network surrounds the alveoli for gas exchange and does not secrete polypeptide hormones. Tell: the paraneoplastic hormones of small cell carcinoma come from neuroendocrine cells in the lining of the bronchioles.

Correct. Neuroendocrine cells are among the cells lining the bronchioles. When small cell carcinoma develops from these cells, which secrete polypeptide hormones, it produces neuroendocrine paraneoplastic symptoms, such as excess antidiuretic hormone with hyponatremia.

set1.q: Papilledema on fundoscopic examination in a patient with lung cancer suggests metastasis to which organ?
opts: Correct. Brain metastasis causes headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncopal episodes and seizures. Raised intracranial pressure adds papilledema and other changes on fundoscopic examination, and a lesion near the midbrain or pons can affect the cranial nerves that move the eyes.

Liver metastasis gives a dull right upper quadrant ache, firm hepatomegaly, jaundice and hepatic failure, not changes at the optic disc. Tell: papilledema reflects raised intracranial pressure, a brain finding.

Adrenal metastasis causes adrenal insufficiency with fatigue, dizziness, hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Tell: a swollen optic disc means raised pressure inside the skull, which points to the brain.

Spinal bone metastasis causes pain, fractures even from a cough, and cord compression with neurologic dysfunction, but not papilledema. Tell: papilledema is seen on fundoscopy when intracranial pressure rises from brain metastasis.

set1.q: How do packs smoked per day and years of smoking affect lung cancer risk?
opts: Correct. Packs per day and years of smoking compound the risk, which climbs from five-fold to ten-fold to twenty-fold and beyond as exposure builds. That is why the screening criterion is written as a pack-year history, a measure that combines the two.

Duration counts as much as intensity: packs per day and years of smoking both compound the risk, five-fold to ten-fold to twenty-fold. Tell: the screening history is counted in pack-years, which captures both how much and how long a person smoked.

The risk does not level off with time; packs per day and years of smoking keep compounding it, five-fold to ten-fold to twenty-fold and beyond. Tell: every added year and every added pack multiplies the risk further.

Quitting does not wipe the risk out at once: people who quit within the last 15 years still qualify for annual low-dose screening because they remain high risk. Tell: a recent former smoker is still screened; the risk built up by packs and years lingers.

set1.q: In what share of lung cancer cases is smoking implicated?
opts: Twenty percent is the figure listed for second-hand smoke, not for smoking overall, which is implicated in 85 to 90% of cases. Tell: the small number belongs to second-hand exposure; direct smoking accounts for the large majority of cases.
Half understates the role of smoking, which is implicated in 85 to 90% of lung cancer cases and is why a heavy smoking history drives screening. Tell: think nearly nine cases in ten, not one in two.

Correct. Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of lung cancer cases, with second-hand smoke listed at 20%, and packs per day and years of smoking compound the risk. Most patients are over 50 with a smoking history, though smoking is not always associated with lung cancer.

Smoking is not behind every case: it is implicated in 85 to 90%, and smoking is not always associated with lung cancer. Radon, air pollution, chemical toxins and genetics are other listed risks. Tell: roughly one case in ten arises without smoking.

set1.q: Which lymph node involvement automatically moves lung cancer to at least stage 3?
opts: Hilar nodes on the tumor side
Hilar nodes on the side of the tumor are N1, and N1 with a tumor up to 5 cm stays in stage 2B. Tell: hilar nodes on the opposite side would be N3, but same-side hilar nodes are not the trigger.

Intrapulmonary nodes are grouped with the peribronchial and hilar nodes on the side of the tumor as N1. Tell: mediastinal nodes (N2) or contralateral and supraclavicular nodes (N3) are what force stage 3.

Correct. N2 or N3 disease, mediastinal or contralateral lymph involvement, automatically moves lung cancer to stage 3. N2 is same-side mediastinal or subcarinal nodes; N3 is contralateral mediastinal or hilar nodes, or any scalene or supraclavicular node.
Peribronchial nodes on the side of the tumor are N1, which with a tumor up to 5 cm gives stage 2B rather than stage 3. Tell: the stage 3 trigger is mediastinal or contralateral spread.

set1.q: Which nodule appearance is concerning for malignancy?
opts: Fatty tissue inside a nodule points to a hamartoma, a benign lesion, as does a smoothly marginated nodule with internal fat and calcification on computed tomography. Tell: fat reassures; a spiky border worries.

Correct. A spiculated appearance, with spikes, deviations or lobulations in the border, is one of the concerning nodule features; the invasive adenocarcinoma example is a suspicious solid spiculated nodule. Other concerning features include size over 6 mm, upper lobe or hilar location and growth over time.
Well-defined borders are a feature of benign nodules, the opposite of a spiculated edge. Tell: a crisp, smooth edge reassures, while spikes, deviations and lobulations in the border raise concern.
Popcorn calcification marks a hamartoma and sits among the benign calcification patterns with diffuse, central and concentric. Tell: popcorn calcium is benign; a spiculated border is concerning.

set1.q: What is the standard management of stage 1 or 2 non-small cell lung cancer?
opts: Radiation is an adjunct for non-small cell cancer, which responds poorly to it; it becomes the main treatment when a patient is unfit for surgery. Tell: a fit patient with stage 1 or 2 disease gets resection.
Immunotherapy is used by marker, with or after chemotherapy, or for patients who are not surgical candidates, such as those with stage 4 disease. Tell: early, resectable disease goes to surgery.

Correct. Standard management for stages 1A through 2B is surgical resection, chosen by size and lymph involvement: a wedge or segment resection or a lobectomy, open or thoracoscopic, or a pneumonectomy. The patient must be able to tolerate surgery, meaning survive it and recover.
Non-small cell lung cancers do not respond well to chemotherapy, which serves as an adjunct to surgery or as treatment in stage 4. Tell: early stages are cut out, not treated with drugs alone.

set1.q: Which is a chronic effect of lung radiotherapy?
opts: Erythema and hyperpigmentation of the skin, with a risk of ulceration, are acute localized effects of radiotherapy. Tell: the chronic change is fibrosis and scarring.
Inflammation is listed among the acute effects of radiotherapy, not the chronic ones. Tell: the lasting damage later on is fibrosis of the lung and of the heart.
Radiotherapy has fewer systemic effects than chemotherapy, so nausea and vomiting are typically limited. Tell: the chronic lung effect is pulmonary fibrosis.

Correct. Chronic effects of lung radiotherapy include pulmonary fibrosis and scarring of the treated tissue, cardiovascular fibrosis with coronary disease, valve disease or cardiomyopathy, localized hair loss, lymphedema from lymphatic damage, and neuropathy.

set1.q: What makes lung cancer one of the more deadly cancers?
opts: Correct. Lung cancer is more deadly than many cancers because patients do not present with symptoms until the disease is advanced or already metastatic. That late presentation helps explain a five-year survival of 17 to 18% in the United States and the case for screening high-risk people without symptoms.

The reverse is true: most incidental nodules are benign, mainly granulomas or hamartomas, although high-risk patients still need workup to exclude malignancy. Tell: lung cancer is deadly because it stays silent until late, not because every nodule is cancer.

Tissue can be taken by bronchoscopy, transthoracic or thoracoscopic biopsy depending on the location of the nodule, and the biopsy can be guided by computed tomography. Tell: diagnosis is possible; the problem is that symptoms arrive late.

Lung cancer spreads readily, to regional nodes and then the liver, brain and bone, and over 70% of small cell carcinomas are metastatic before detection. Tell: late symptoms and early spread go together.

set1.q: Which paraneoplastic finding is linked particularly to squamous cell carcinoma?
opts: Hyponatremia with low serum osmolality comes from excess antidiuretic hormone produced by small cell carcinoma. Tell: low sodium points to small cell; high calcium points to squamous.
Flushing belongs to carcinoid syndrome, from serotonin released by a bronchial carcinoid. Tell: the paraneoplastic marker of squamous cell carcinoma is hypercalcemia.
Progressive leg weakness is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, a neurologic paraneoplastic syndrome. Tell: the endocrine syndrome tied to squamous cell carcinoma is hypercalcemia.

Correct. Paraneoplastic syndromes come from secreted hormonal or cytokine effects of tumor tissue, and hypercalcemia is the endocrine syndrome linked particularly to squamous cell carcinoma. Calcium is measured on the comprehensive metabolic panel in the lab workup.

set1.q: Who is the lung cancer screening recommendation meant for?
opts: A known nodule takes a patient outside screening; it is followed or worked up as a nodule, by its size, appearance and the patient's risk. Tell: screening looks for nodules in people with no known nodule and no symptoms.
ruled out by a stated finding
Hemoptysis is a symptom, and patients who present with symptoms are worked up for possible lung cancer rather than screened. Tell: screening is for people without symptoms.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for certain high-risk individuals without symptoms or a known nodule, a benefit shown in the National Lung Cancer Screening Trial. High risk means the age band plus a heavy pack-year history in someone who smokes now or quit within the last 15 years.

A smoking history alone is not enough: screening is for high-risk adults within the age band with a heavy pack-year history who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years. Tell: a light or long-past smoking history does not qualify.

set1.q: A 2 cm lung cancer has spread to mediastinal lymph nodes on the same side, with no distant metastasis; which stage is it?
opts: Stage 2B allows nodal spread only to peribronchial or hilar nodes with a tumor up to 5 cm. Tell: mediastinal nodes automatically move the cancer into stage 3.

Correct. A tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the mediastinal lymph nodes, subcarinal nodes included, on the side of the tumor is stage 3A. Mediastinal involvement, N2, automatically moves a cancer to stage 3, whatever the size of the tumor.

Stage 3B is a tumor over 5 cm with mediastinal nodes, or a tumor up to 5 cm with nodes on the side without the tumor or with supraclavicular or scalene nodes. Tell: a small tumor with same-side mediastinal nodes is stage 3A.
Stage 3C is a tumor over 5 cm with contralateral, supraclavicular or scalene nodes. Tell: this tumor is small and its nodes are same-side mediastinal, which is stage 3A.

set1.q: Which lung cancer has the strongest association with smoking?
opts: Small cell carcinoma is a central type tied to neuroendocrine paraneoplastic syndromes and to a lesion of the short arm of chromosome 3. Tell: the strongest smoking link belongs to squamous cell carcinoma.
Large cell carcinoma is a rare, peripheral diagnosis of exclusion that can spread to the bowel. Tell: the strongest association with smoking points to squamous cell carcinoma.

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma, the second most common lung cancer, has the strongest association with smoking. It is central, often arises in a bronchus and shows frequent cavitation and obstruction, with cough, wheezing and hemoptysis once the bronchus is blocked.
Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer, and smoking is not always associated with it. Tell: the type most tightly tied to smoking is squamous cell carcinoma.

set1.q: A 2.5 cm lung cancer has not spread to any lymph nodes or distant sites; which stage is it?
opts: Correct. Stage 1A is a tumor no more than 3 cm in its greatest dimension that has not spread to any lymph nodes. At 2.5 cm with no nodes and no metastasis, this tumor is T1 N0 M0; all stage 1 to 3 tumors are free of distant metastasis.
Stage 1B is a node-negative tumor more than 3 cm but no more than 4 cm in its greatest dimension. Tell: 2.5 cm is under the 3 cm line, so this node-negative tumor stays in stage 1A.
Stage 2A is a node-negative tumor more than 4 cm but no more than 5 cm in its greatest dimension. Tell: a 2.5 cm tumor is far below that range, and with no nodes it stays in stage 1A.

Stage 2B is a node-negative tumor of more than 5 to 7 cm, or one that has grown into nearby sites, or a tumor up to 5 cm with peribronchial or hilar nodes. Tell: this tumor is small and node-negative, so it is stage 1A.

set1.q: After a response to initial therapy, which lung cancer is offered prophylactic cranial irradiation?
opts: Correct. In small cell carcinoma with a complete or partial response to initial therapy, prophylactic cranial irradiation is recommended in limited stage and considered, with or without thoracic radiotherapy, in extensive stage. Brain magnetic resonance imaging is the preferred scan of the brain.
Adenocarcinoma is non-small cell and is treated by stage, with resection in early stages and chemotherapy in stage 4. Tell: preventive irradiation of the brain belongs to the small cell pathway.
Squamous cell carcinoma is a central non-small cell type whose management combines surgery, chemotherapy and radiation. Tell: the brain is irradiated preventively in small cell carcinoma.

Large cell carcinoma is kept apart from small cell carcinoma precisely because their treatments differ, and it has no standardized treatment. Tell: prophylactic cranial irradiation is a small cell treatment.

set2.q: Which change in a nodule over time is concerning?
opts: Central calcification is one of the benign patterns, typical of a healed granuloma, so it reassures rather than worries. Tell: growth over time is the concerning change.

Correct. A nodule that is enlarging in size over time is a concerning feature, together with size over 6 mm, upper lobe or hilar location, a spiculated border, more than three nodules, contrast enhancement and a cavitated or nonsolid appearance.
A nodule that holds its size does not meet the growth criterion; enlargement over time is what raises concern. Tell: the warning sign is a change in size, specifically growth.
Shrinkage is the opposite of the concerning change; the listed feature is a nodule enlarging in size over time, alongside size over 6 mm and a spiculated border. Tell: growth worries, not regression.

set2.q: A lung cancer of any size has spread to one site outside the chest, the adrenal gland; which stage is it?
opts: All stage 1 to 3 tumors are free of distant metastasis, and stage 3B is defined by tumor size and nodal spread alone. Tell: any spread outside the chest, even to one adrenal gland, makes it stage 4.
Stage 3C is the furthest nodal stage without metastasis, a tumor over 5 cm with contralateral, supraclavicular or scalene nodes. Tell: an adrenal metastasis jumps past stage 3 to stage 4.

Correct. Stage 4A covers spread to the other lung, into the lining of the lung or heart with secondary nodules, into the fluid around the lungs or heart, or to one site outside the chest, such as the adrenal gland. Spread to multiple sites outside the chest would make it stage 4B.
Stage 4B means spread to multiple sites outside the chest, such as the adrenal gland and the bones. Tell: one extrathoracic site is 4A; more than one is 4B.

set2.q: A smoothly marginated solid nodule with central calcification on computed tomography is typical of what?
opts: A hamartoma is also smoothly marginated, but its tell is internal fat with calcification, often popcorn-looking. Tell: central calcification alone suggests a healed granuloma.

Invasive adenocarcinoma appears as a suspicious solid spiculated nodule in the periphery, not a smooth nodule with central calcification. Tell: smooth margins plus central calcium is a benign picture.
A linear scar or lymphoid tissue is the nodular opacity lying next to the minor fissure, not a calcified nodule. Tell: a fissure-side opacity means scar; central calcification means healed granuloma.

Correct. A smoothly marginated solid nodule with central calcification is typical of a healed granuloma, an inflammatory lesion and one of the two main benign nodules. Central calcification is also one of the benign calcification patterns, with diffuse, popcorn and concentric.

set2.q: In the diagnostic workup of a lung nodule or lung cancer symptoms, which imaging is standard before biopsy?
opts: Low-dose chest computed tomography is the annual screening test for high-risk adults without symptoms or a known nodule, and the noncontrast surveillance scan for a very low probability nodule. Tell: screening and surveillance use the low-dose scan; the diagnostic study before biopsy is contrast scanning of the chest and upper abdomen.

Magnetic resonance imaging is the preferred brain scan before prophylactic cranial irradiation in small cell carcinoma, not the standard chest study. Tell: the diagnostic workup of a lung nodule starts with contrast computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen.

Correct. The standard is computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen, followed by biopsy or interventional treatment; positron emission tomography and genetic testing are also part of the standard workup. A chest radiograph is not a good tool here.

A chest radiograph may be the first test to show a nodule, but it is not a good tool for the workup and otherwise serves to rule out other pathology. Tell: in the diagnostic workup of a nodule or symptoms, the standard is contrast computed tomography.

set2.q: In lung cancer, fatigue, weight loss, dizziness, hypotension and a high potassium point to metastasis where?
opts: Correct. Metastasis that causes adrenal insufficiency produces fatigue, weight loss, dizziness, hypotension and electrolyte imbalance, hyponatremia with hyperkalemia, often with no respiratory symptoms at all. The high potassium with low blood pressure is the clue that separates it from the other metastatic sites.

Brain metastasis causes headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncopal episodes and seizures, with papilledema if intracranial pressure rises. Tell: hypotension with a high potassium points to the adrenal glands, not the brain.

Liver metastasis causes a dull right upper quadrant ache, firm hepatomegaly, poor appetite, jaundice and eventually hepatic failure. Tell: electrolyte changes with hypotension point to adrenal insufficiency instead.

Bone metastasis, including the spine, causes bone pain, fractures without falls and spinal cord compression with neurologic dysfunction. Tell: a high potassium and hypotension are adrenal findings, not skeletal ones.

set2.q: A nodular opacity lying next to the minor fissure on computed tomography is typical of what?
opts: Correct. A nodular opacity adjacent to the minor fissure is typical of a linear scar or lymphoid tissue, and a nodule close to a fissure usually indicates something benign. It is one of the benign computed tomography findings, with the hamartoma and the healed granuloma.
Invasive adenocarcinoma is the suspicious solid spiculated nodule in the lung periphery. Tell: a small opacity hugging a fissure is usually benign scar or lymphoid tissue.
Satellite nodules are extra nodules in the same lobe as a known primary tumor, a T3 staging feature. Tell: with no primary tumor, an opacity beside the fissure suggests scar or lymphoid tissue.
A healed granuloma is a smoothly marginated solid nodule with central calcification, not an opacity lying along the fissure. Tell: fissure-side opacities are scars or lymphoid tissue.

set2.q: A lung cancer has spread to both the adrenal gland and the bones; which stage is it?
opts: Stage 3B is a nodal stage without metastasis, since all stage 1 to 3 tumors are M0; it is set by tumor size and lymph node spread. Tell: spread to the bones and the adrenal gland means stage 4.
Stage 3C still has no distant metastasis; it is a large tumor with contralateral, supraclavicular or scalene nodes. Tell: distant organs involved means stage 4.
Stage 4A allows one site outside the chest, or spread to the other lung, the pleura, the pericardium or the fluid around them. Tell: two extrathoracic sites, adrenal plus bone, make it stage 4B.

Correct. Stage 4B is a tumor of any size, with or without nodal spread, that has spread to multiple sites outside the chest, such as the adrenal gland and the bones. Spread to only one site outside the chest would be stage 4A.

set2.q: Neuroendocrine paraneoplastic symptoms arise when a lung carcinoma develops from cells that secrete polypeptide hormones; which type does this?
opts: Correct. Small cell carcinoma can develop neuroendocrine paraneoplastic symptoms when it arises from cells that secrete polypeptide hormones, the neuroendocrine cells lining the bronchioles. Paraneoplastic syndromes are typically a consequence of the small cell type, such as excess antidiuretic hormone with hyponatremia.

Adenocarcinoma arises from type II pneumocytes, the surfactant-secreting cells, and its paraneoplastic issues appear only as late systemic signs. Tell: hormone-secreting neuroendocrine cells give rise to the symptoms of small cell carcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma is linked particularly to hypercalcemia, but it arises in the bronchus, not from hormone-secreting neuroendocrine cells. Tell: the neuroendocrine paraneoplastic type is small cell.

A hamartoma is a benign connective tissue growth, often with fat or popcorn calcification, not a carcinoma that secretes hormones. Tell: neuroendocrine paraneoplastic symptoms point to small cell carcinoma.

set2.q: What is the first evaluation of a lung nodule found incidentally on imaging done for another reason?
opts: Sputum cytology is an additional test that is not sensitive, so it does not open the evaluation of an incidental nodule. Tell: the opening step is measuring the nodule, since one under 6 mm is usually not concerning.

A chest radiograph is not a good tool for working up a nodule beyond first spotting it; it mainly serves to rule out other pathology. Tell: the first evaluation is the size estimate, judged against the 6 mm mark.

Correct. Incidental nodules turn up on a chest radiograph or chest computed tomography done for another reason, and the first evaluation is to estimate size. Anything smaller than 6 mm is generally not concerning unless the patient is at high risk, while a nodule over 6 mm draws attention.

Biopsy comes later, after imaging and risk assessment point toward malignancy; most incidental nodules are benign, mainly granulomas or hamartomas. Tell: size the nodule first, then decide whether tissue is needed.

set2.q: Besides regional lymph nodes, to which organs does lung cancer typically spread?
opts: These are not among the named distant sites. Lung cancer spreads to the liver, brain and bone, and each of those has its own metastatic signs, such as firm hepatomegaly, papilledema and fractures without falls. Tell: remember liver, brain and bone.

Breast and ovary are not the distant targets named for lung cancer; spread runs to the regional nodes and then the liver, brain and bone. Tell: metastatic lung cancer can present with no respiratory symptoms at all, through liver, brain or bone complaints.

Correct. Lung cancer spreads to regional lymph nodes and then to distant organs, the liver, brain and bone, as it produces new blood vessels to exceed its boundaries and its cells become poorly differentiated. Over 70% of small cell carcinomas have already reached the liver, bone or brain by detection.

Spread to the small intestine and bowel is the unusual pattern of large cell carcinoma, one of its distinctive features, not the usual destination of lung cancer. Tell: the usual distant sites are liver, brain and bone; the gut points to large cell.

set2.q: Why is small cell carcinoma usually metastatic before it is detected?
opts: Small cell describes the tumor cells, small with no nucleoli and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio, not a small tumor. Tell: the delay comes from insidious infiltration of the mucosa.
Limited-stage small cell carcinoma involves local lymph nodes, so the tumor does not skip them. Tell: late detection reflects insidious growth along the mucosa.

Correct. Small cell carcinoma is central and infiltrates the mucosa, which makes its development insidious, so over 70% of patients are metastatic, to the liver, bone or brain, before detection. Once the tumor is large enough for symptoms it also has a high cavitation rate.
Small cell carcinoma is central, not peripheral; adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma are the peripheral types. Tell: it hides because it infiltrates the mucosa and grows insidiously.

set2.q: Biopsy confirms stage 1 non-small cell lung cancer in a patient who is not fit for surgery; which treatment follows?
opts: Lobectomy is the resection for a surgical candidate with confirmed malignancy, and stage 1 disease is usually resected. Tell: a patient unfit for surgery cannot have any resection, so treatment moves to radiotherapy or ablation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Anatomical segmentectomy is for a patient fit for surgery but unfit for lobectomy; it is still an operation. Tell: a patient unfit for any surgery is treated with radiotherapy or ablation instead.
ruled out by a stated finding

A wedge resection with on-table frozen section is a surgical option for a patient who is fit for surgery. Tell: when surgery is not possible, treatment shifts to stereotactic or conventional radiotherapy or radiofrequency ablation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Resection requires a patient who can tolerate surgery. When a patient is unfit, image-guided biopsy is done if possible and safe, and confirmed malignancy is treated with stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation or conventional radical radiotherapy; if biopsy is unsafe, those treatments proceed anyway.

set2.q: Why do chemotherapy and radiation serve mainly as adjuncts in non-small cell lung cancer?
opts: The reverse is true: about two thirds of adenocarcinoma patients present with advanced or metastatic disease, and lung cancer stays silent until late. Tell: the adjunct role reflects poor response, not early detection.

Correct. Chemotherapy and radiation are an adjunct to surgery, or used in stage 4, because non-small cell lung cancers do not respond well to them. Small cell carcinoma is the contrast: it responds better to chemotherapy and radiation than the three non-small cell types.

Pulmonary fibrosis and scarring are chronic effects of lung radiotherapy, but they are not why these treatments are adjuncts here. Tell: the reason is the cancer's poor response, unlike small cell carcinoma.

Chemotherapy and immunotherapy can now be targeted to genetic and protein markers, which refines these treatments rather than replacing them. Tell: they stay adjuncts because the tumor responds poorly.

set2.q: Excess antidiuretic hormone from small cell lung cancer produces which sodium and osmolality pattern?
opts: Retained water dilutes the blood, so sodium and osmolality both fall rather than rise. Tell: too much antidiuretic hormone means too much water, which pushes both values down.
Sodium does fall, but serum osmolality falls with it because the excess is water. Tell: both values move down together when antidiuretic hormone is in excess.
Water retention lowers the sodium rather than raising it, while osmolality also drops. Tell: hyponatremia with decreased serum osmolality is the pattern.

Correct. Excess antidiuretic hormone, vasopressin, makes the body retain too much water, so hyponatremia and decreased serum osmolality result. These cause confusion, seizures, ataxia and other neurologic dysfunction, without peripheral or pulmonary edema.

set2.q: What is the main downside of annual lung cancer screening?
opts: Finding cancer early is the upside of screening, not its downside; early detection leads to rapid intervention and an improved prognosis. Tell: the problem is finding too much, false positives, not too little.
Low-dose computed tomography deliberately uses less radiation than a standard chest scan to reduce exposure. Tell: the drawback is false positives that lead to unnecessary workup.
Screening speeds treatment, since early detection leads to rapid intervention. Tell: the cost of screening is benign findings that trigger unnecessary workup and its complications.

Correct. Screening has a high incidence of false positives that prove benign, so patients receive an unnecessary workup that could have complications, such as those of a biopsy. The upside is early detection, which allows rapid intervention and an improved prognosis.

set2.q: In which stage of small cell carcinoma does radiation work best?
opts: Radiation does not work equally at every stage; it works best in limited stage, confined to one area with local lymph nodes involved. Tell: the more confined the disease, the better radiation works.

Correct. Small cell carcinoma is divided by metastasis into limited stage, confined to one area with only local lymph nodes involved, extensive stage, spread away from the local area, and combined. Radiation works best when the cancer is in limited stage.
Extensive stage has spread away from the local area. Tell: radiation works best while the disease is confined, in limited stage.

Combined small cell carcinoma means different histological types mixed with non-small cell cancer, and it is not the category named for the best radiation response. Tell: radiation works best in limited stage, confined to one area with only local lymph nodes involved.

set2.q: What do carcinogens do to oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in lung cells?
opts: Activating tumor suppressor genes would restrain growth, not release it; in lung cancer those genes are inactivated by further mutation or loss of regulatory control. Tell: the oncogenes are switched on and the suppressors are switched off.

Inactivating oncogenes would slow growth, the opposite of what carcinogens do; they activate oncogenes while the tumor suppressor genes are lost. Tell: cancer needs the accelerator on and the brake off.

Correct. Carcinogens, or other causes of genetic mutation, activate oncogenes in lung cells, and further mutations or loss of regulatory control inactivate the tumor suppressor genes. Together these let atypical cells proliferate and grow, starting locally and then spreading.

This reverses both changes. Carcinogens switch oncogenes on and switch tumor suppressor genes off, which frees atypical cells to proliferate. Tell: growth genes turned on plus brakes turned off gives unchecked growth.

set2.q: What are solitary nodules seen on a chest radiograph sometimes called?
opts: Ground-glass describes how a nodule looks, as a stippled calcification pattern grouped with the malignant patterns and as a subsolid nodule type tracked on computed tomography, not the name for a solitary nodule on a chest radiograph. Tell: ground-glass describes a texture; coin lesion describes a solitary nodule.

Correct. A solitary nodule seen on a chest radiograph is sometimes called a coin lesion. Most such nodules are benign, mainly granulomas or hamartomas, but a patient at high risk for lung cancer needs screening and workup to exclude malignancy.

Satellite nodules are additional nodules in the same lobe as a primary tumor, a T3 feature in staging, not a name for a single nodule on a chest film. Tell: satellite implies more than one nodule; coin lesion means a solitary one.

Popcorn describes a calcification pattern, the popcorn look of a hamartoma, not the general name for a solitary nodule. Tell: popcorn names how calcium looks inside a nodule; coin lesion names the solitary nodule itself.

set2.q: Local invasion by squamous cell carcinoma toward the laryngeal nerves causes which later sign?
opts: Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma metastasizes by local invasion, producing later signs such as dysphagia and voice changes when it spreads to the laryngeal nerves. Its earlier symptoms, cough, wheezing and hemoptysis, follow obstruction of the bronchus.
Papilledema reflects raised intracranial pressure from brain metastasis. Tell: invasion of the laryngeal nerves changes the voice, not the optic disc.
Progressive leg weakness is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, an autoimmune attack on calcium channels at nerve endings. Tell: laryngeal nerve invasion affects the voice, not the legs.
Cutaneous flushing is a carcinoid syndrome sign, driven by serotonin from a bronchial carcinoid. Tell: local invasion of the laryngeal nerves causes voice changes.

set2.q: A central lung cancer that cavitates, obstructs a bronchus and raises the serum calcium is most likely which type?
opts: Large cell carcinoma does cavitate, but it forms in the periphery and spreads to the bowel. Tell: a central, obstructing, calcium-raising tumor is squamous.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma is central, often arising in the bronchus, with frequent cavitation and obstruction, and hypercalcemia is the paraneoplastic syndrome linked particularly to it. The raised calcium is the clue that separates it from the other central type, small cell carcinoma.

Small cell carcinoma is also central and can cavitate once large, but its classic endocrine syndrome is excess antidiuretic hormone with hyponatremia. Tell: high calcium points to squamous, low sodium to small cell.
Adenocarcinoma sits in the mid-lung and periphery, so a central obstructing mass does not fit it. Tell: central location plus a high calcium means squamous.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: For a new solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm with a low-to-moderate clinical probability of malignancy, what is the next step?
opts: Surveillance scans at 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 24 months are where a very low probability nodule goes directly, and where a low-to-moderate nodule goes only after negative or mild uptake. Tell: the middle group needs the tracer scan first.

Resection by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is the high-probability path after staging, or follows intense uptake; it is not the first step for a low-to-moderate nodule. Tell: the middle group is sorted by tracer uptake before anyone operates.
Sputum cytology is an additional test that is not sensitive. Tell: the low-to-moderate group is sorted by its uptake on positron emission tomography.

Correct. A low-to-moderate probability nodule is assessed with fludeoxyglucose positron emission tomography. Negative or mild uptake sends it to surveillance scans; moderate or intense uptake leads to nonsurgical biopsy or video-assisted thoracoscopic resection, with subspecialist referral.

set2.q: Which nodule appearance suggests that it is benign?
opts: Lobulations in the border fall under the concerning spiculated appearance, alongside spikes and deviations. Tell: an irregular, lobulated edge raises concern, while a well-defined edge reassures.
A cavitated or nonsolid appearance is on the list of concerning nodule features. Tell: cavitation worries; well-defined borders, fat and benign calcification patterns reassure.

Correct. Benign nodules tend to have well-defined borders, and they may contain fatty tissue or popcorn-looking calcification, both pointing to a hamartoma. On computed tomography the benign examples are smoothly marginated solid nodules.
A spiculated border, with spikes or deviations, is a concerning feature that points toward malignancy. Tell: the benign border is crisp and well defined.

set2.q: About what share of lung cancers occur in people under 40 years old?
opts: Correct. Most lung cancers occur in people over 50, but about 4% occur in people under 40. The share is small but real, so a young age alone does not exclude lung cancer in a patient with persistent cough, hemoptysis or weight loss.

Fifteen percent overstates the young share: about 4% of lung cancers occur in people under 40, and most occur in people over 50. Tell: 15 to 20% is the share of small cell carcinoma among all lung cancers, a different figure.
A quarter would make lung cancer common in young adults, but most cases occur in people over 50 and about 4% in people under 40. Tell: the under-40 share is a single-digit percentage.
Forty percent mixes up the age cutoff with the share. About 4% of lung cancers occur in people under 40, while most occur in people over 50. Tell: the age is 40; the percentage is 4.

set2.q: Which step comes directly before an invasive malignant tumor in lung cancer growth?
opts: Metastases form at distant sites after the malignant tumor has invaded normal tissue and entered blood and lymph, so they come after invasion, not before it. Tell: in situ cancer is the step before invasion; metastasis is the step after.

Correct. Growth runs from a genetically altered epithelial cell to hyperplasia, where cells divide faster than normal, then dysplasia, where cells change form, then in situ cancer, where cells stay in one place. Next comes the malignant tumor that invades normal tissue and enters blood and lymph.

Hyperplasia, cells dividing more rapidly than normal, is the first change after the genetically altered cell, three steps before invasion. Tell: just before invasion the cells are already cancer but still stay in one place, in situ.
Dysplasia, where the cells change form, comes before in situ cancer, not directly before invasion. Tell: the order is hyperplasia, dysplasia, in situ cancer, then the invasive malignant tumor.

set2.q: Which central lung cancer can be diagnosed with sputum cytology?
opts: Small cell carcinoma is also central, but it infiltrates the mucosa and is usually metastatic by the time of diagnosis; sputum testing is not its noted route to diagnosis. Tell: of the two central types, squamous is the one found in sputum.
Adenocarcinoma is peripheral, not central; sputum cytology is not its diagnostic route. Tell: a central tumor found in sputum is squamous.
ruled out by a stated finding
Large cell carcinoma is peripheral and a diagnosis of exclusion that still needs biopsy with histology. Tell: sputum diagnosis belongs to central squamous cell carcinoma.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma arises in the central bronchi, and unlike the other lung cancers it can be caught with sputum testing, even though sputum cytology is otherwise not sensitive. Its bronchial origin is also why cough, wheezing and hemoptysis appear once it obstructs.

set2.q: Which peripheral lung cancer metastasizes to unusual sites such as the small intestine and bowel?
opts: Small cell carcinoma is central and has spread to the liver, bone or brain before detection in over 70% of patients. Tell: its central location and usual sites rule it out; small intestine and bowel point to large cell.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Large cell carcinoma forms in the periphery and can metastasize to rare areas such as the small intestine and bowel, a feature that sets it apart. It is anaplastic and undifferentiated, forms necrosis and hemorrhage readily and shows a large cavitated mass on computed tomography.
Adenocarcinoma is also peripheral, but its initial metastases go to the lymphatics before it advances out of the lungs. Tell: the gut as a metastatic site is the large cell signature.

Squamous cell carcinoma is central and spreads by local invasion, causing dysphagia and voice changes, and by lymphangitic spread to hilar nodes. Tell: it is not peripheral, and bowel spread belongs to large cell.

set2.q: In tumor, node and metastasis staging of lung cancer, what does N1 describe?
opts: Correct. N1 is spread to ipsilateral, same-side, peribronchial or hilar nodes and intrapulmonary nodes. N2 is same-side mediastinal or subcarinal nodes, and N3 is contralateral mediastinal or hilar nodes or any scalene or supraclavicular node.
Same-side mediastinal or subcarinal nodes are N2, which automatically moves the cancer to stage 3. Tell: N1 stays within the lung and hilum on the side of the tumor.
Contralateral hilar nodes are N3, not N1, and N3 disease automatically moves the cancer to stage 3. Tell: crossing to the other side of the chest is a later, worse nodal category than N1.
Any scalene or supraclavicular node, on either side, is N3. Tell: N1 is limited to peribronchial, hilar and intrapulmonary nodes on the side of the tumor.

opts: Nonsurgical biopsy, by transthoracic needle or endoscopy, follows moderate or intense uptake on positron emission tomography in the low-to-moderate group. Tell: tissue is sought once uptake raises concern, while a very low probability nodule is watched.

Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection ends the high-probability path once staging finds no metastases, or follows intense uptake. Tell: resection matches high probability; surveillance matches very low probability.

Positron emission tomography is the step for a low-to-moderate probability nodule; a very low probability nodule goes straight to surveillance scans. Tell: very low probability means watching with serial computed tomography, while the middle group gets the tracer scan.

set2.q: What is lepidic growth in adenocarcinoma?
opts: Correct. After starting as atypical adenomatous hyperplasia and growing in situ, adenocarcinoma either enlarges by lepidic growth across the alveolar lining or begins to invade the stroma. Stromal invasion defines minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, and pleural and vascular invasion define invasive disease.
Invading the stroma is the alternative path, and it defines minimally invasive adenocarcinoma. Tell: lepidic growth spreads across the surface of the alveolar lining instead of into the stroma.
Pleural invasion, followed by vascular invasion or new vessel formation, marks an invasive adenocarcinoma, a later step than lepidic growth. Tell: lepidic means surface spread along the alveoli.

Lymphangitic spread into hilar nodes describes squamous cell carcinoma, and adenocarcinoma's first metastases go to the lymphatics. Tell: lepidic growth is local surface growth along the alveolar lining, not nodal spread.

set2.q: Which lung cancer type is also called oat cell carcinoma?
opts: Correct. Small cell lung carcinoma is also called oat cell carcinoma and makes up 15 to 20% of lung cancers. It is the type that typically produces paraneoplastic syndromes, sits centrally and is usually metastatic by the time of diagnosis.

Large cell carcinoma is a non-small cell type with cells about three times larger than baseline, kept apart from small cell carcinoma because the treatments differ. Tell: oat cell names the small cell type, the opposite end of the size scale.

Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common lung cancer, a central non-small cell type with the strongest link to smoking, and oat cell is not its name. Tell: oat cell is the other name for small cell carcinoma.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer, a non-small cell type that arises from type II pneumocytes in the mid-lung and periphery. Tell: the oat cell name belongs to small cell carcinoma, the other main type.
